title: The Cold War and the Bomb

cards.h: Thirteen days when the world nearly ended
cards.b:
In October 1962, the US found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 150 km from Florida. For 13 days the two superpowers stared at each other.

That was the Cold War: no direct war between the US and USSR, but constant fear, spies, proxy wars and enough bombs to wreck the planet.
The wartime allies split over Eastern Europe. The US offered the Truman Doctrine (1947) and Marshall Plan to resist communism. The USSR built a bloc of satellite states.
The superpowers never fought directly. They fought through others: Korea (1950-53), Vietnam, Afghanistan. The doctrine of Mutual Assured Destruction held that a nuclear attack would destroy both.

During the Cuban crisis a Soviet submarine officer, Vasili Arkhipov, reportedly refused to agree to fire a nuclear torpedo. In 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov judged a missile alarm to be false and did not report it as an attack.

Historians agree these were real near-misses, though details are debated.

Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed that the USSR would remove missiles from Cuba and the US would pledge not to invade. A secret part of the deal: the US would withdraw missiles from Turkey later.

A hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up in 1963.

cards.h: Did the US simply win by staring down the Soviets?
cards.b:
Myth: Kennedy forced a Soviet retreat with no concessions.Fact: the secret Turkey deal was kept hidden for years. Both sides compromised.

Also, 'Cold' is misleading: millions died in proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola and elsewhere.

Neither camp

India chose to stay out of both blocs. Nehru said the country would not join either side. In 1954 India and China signed the Panchsheel principles. In 1955 Nehru was at Bandung, and in 1961 he was one of the founders of the Non-Aligned Movement at Belgrade, with Tito and Nasser.

Non-alignment meant taking help from all sides. The Soviet Union helped build the Bhilai steel plant (1955), and American wheat under the PL-480 scheme fed Indians in the 1950s and 1960s. In 1971 India signed a treaty with the Soviet Union during the Bangladesh crisis, a sign that neutrality had limits.

Five things to remember

  1. The Cold War began after 1945.
  2. NATO (1949) faced the Warsaw Pact (1955).
  3. Wars were fought by proxy.
  4. Cuba 1962 was the closest call.
  5. India led non-alignment.

Think about it

  • Is nuclear deterrence a peace or a gamble?
  • Was non-alignment neutral or just independent?
